web_evidence.title: Looking for Mr. Goodbar by Judith Rossner — ebook preview
web_evidence.note: The licensed ebook preview separates a named opening section, “THE CONFESSION,” containing brief authorial I-comments and Gary’s first-person transcript, from the ensuing sustained third-person account of Theresa’s childhood.

web_evidence.title: Looking for Mr. Goodbar: Reading a Cautionary Tale in Historical Context — Bahar Tahamtani
web_evidence.note: This scholarly close reading identifies the opening as a fictional report and confession, says Rossner spends only twelve pages on White, and states that the remaining 260 pages detail Theresa’s story; this resolves the first-person opening as local material rather than an alternating base strand.

web_evidence.title: Looking for Mr. Goodbar, 40 Years Later
web_evidence.note: Kirkus independently describes the confession as the novel’s opening and distinguishes it from the narrative that follows about Theresa, corroborating the embedded status of the first-person confession.

Opened and inspected the Everand ebook preview, including the named confession, its authorial framing, Gary’s transcript, and the transition into Theresa’s third-person childhood narrative.

Checked Simon & Schuster, Google Books, Open Library, EBSCO, Kirkus, and The New Yorker; publisher and library catalog pages verified the edition but offered little explicit person evidence, while Kirkus corroborated the confession-versus-following-narrative structure.

Targeted searches for epistolary, diary, frame narrative, multiple narrators, and alternating point of view found no evidence of sustained first- or second-person base sections beyond the localized opening confession and brief authorial framing.
person_note: The controlling story is close third-person narration centered on Theresa Dunn, as shown repeatedly by the event quotations and by the main narrative beginning in the authorized preview. The apparent contrary first-person material is confined to the named opening confession: Gary’s speech is an embedded police transcript, while the authorial “I” briefly comments on transcription and interpretation without participating in Theresa’s story. Scholarly structural analysis confirms that this opening occupies about twelve pages and that the remaining 260 pages detail Theresa’s life. Those localized voices therefore do not constitute alternating base narration. The only material limitation is that the authorized prose preview covers the opening rather than the entire novel, but the interior quotations and whole-book scholarly analysis independently close that gap.
